title: Learning to speak where decisions are made: the new School of Advocacy Network
content:
This piece is written by Burak Sayin (Space-time Works) and Niels Righolt (Center for Kunst og Interkultur), reflecting upon the new chapter of the CAE Nordic-Baltic Hub and the Culture Action Europe Nordic-Baltic School of Advocacy Network. 

When we talk about advocacy in the cultural sector, we often imagine a room in Brussels or sector representatives meeting with national cultural authorities. A meeting, a position paper, a moment of access. But the work that makes those moments possible happens much earlier and much closer to home, in the daily conditions of artists and small organisations trying to keep working at all. Building something around that conviction has taken time. We have gone from being an embryo for an interesting conversation to having a framework.

title: Promoting an economy for sustaining a thriving culture in Europe
content:
This essay is written by CAE Board Member Rocío Nogales Muriel, Executive Director of the EMES International Research Network & Vice-President of SmartIb cooperative.

Europe is currently making a series of critical policy decisions that will shape its capacity to respond to the challenges of next decades. Such a process involves, among other things, restructuring key industrial policies and revitalising areas that citizens feel have been left behind. All the while, responding to the return of the war in Europe and steadily rising levels of poverty and inequality in our societies.

All of these decisions are being drawn-up against a majority of European citizens consumed by everyday pressures like paying rent amid skyrocketing housing costs; working multiple jobs; managing mental health issues with their own limited resources and trying to find enough time to care for their loved ones, participate in community life or enjoy leisure and cultural activities.

title: A Sector Contribution to the Work Plan for Culture 2027–2030
content:
Just finished digesting the EU’s new strategic documents for culture, the Culture Compass and the Joint Declaration? Another policy document is coming later this year: the Work Plan for Culture of the Council of the EU 2027-2030.  

Every four years, the culture ministers of the Member States agree on a document that sets out shared priorities for cooperation at EU level. You can think of it as the Council’s to-do list for cultural coordination over the next four years. The Work Plan identifies key topics and then organises practical ways for Member States, the Commission and successive Council Presidencies to work together. In general, the Work Plan produces what we often call ‘soft law’: policy guidance, shared recommendations and knowledge exchange. The document is not legally binding, nor does it directly allocate funding, but it can still shape agendas, national policies and the direction of EU cultural action. 

The next Work Plan will cover 2027–2030 and is expected to be adopted under the Irish Presidency by the end of 2026. The first draft, not publicly available, was presented already on 3 July.

title: 140+ organisations call for a more ambitious budget for culture in AgoraEU
content:
Culture Action Europe has initiated an open letter addressed to EU policymakers on the future of Creative Europe in the next long-term EU budget. More than 140 cultural organisations, networks, and institutions from across Europe have signed the open letter so far, which makes the case for a stronger dedicated Culture strand in the new AgoraEU programme.

Together, we call for at least 25% of the budget of the new AgoraEU programme to be allocated to its cultural component, while also calling for more accessible funding procedures, stronger support for international cultural cooperation, and fair pay and social security guarantees.

title: The other giant in the room: the Council’s Work Plan for Culture
content:
Over the past months, we’ve talked a lot about the European Commission’s work on the Culture Compass and the European Parliament’s efforts to influence the current funding proposals. With negotiations on the next long-term EU budget gathering pace, both institutions are busy trying to shape what comes next for culture. But there is a third player in the room that we cannot afford to overlook: the Council of the EU. 

Let’s keep it simple. 

If the European Commission is the institution that proposes legislations, and manages programmes and fundings, while the European Parliament is the directly elected body representing citizens, the Council of the EU is where national governments sit around the table. It brings together ministers from all Member States to negotiate and adopt EU policies, ensuring that European ambitions remain connected to national realities. 

And yes, culture has a seat at that table too, even though cultural policies remain primarily a national competence. What the EU can do is support cooperation, facilitate exchanges and encourage countries to work together on shared challenges. 

That is precisely where the Work Plan comes in.

title: EU leaders sign ambitious Joint Declaration on Culture
content:
Culture Action Europe welcomes the Joint Declaration ‘Europe for Culture – Culture for Europe‘ co-signed by the leaders of the European Commission, European Parliament, and Council of the EU on 18 June 2026. This marks the first time the EU institutions will unite behind common political commitments for culture. 

The draft Joint Declaration “Europe for Culture – Culture for Europe” accompanied the Culture Compass in November 2025, outlining guiding principles and 12 broad commitments on culture. The document was debated and amended by the European Parliament and Council earlier this year before a provisional interinstitutional agreement was struck in May 2026. While the text has undergone some minor changes since the draft release, the content of the commitments have remained the same: the declaration affirms that culture is central to Europe’s democracy, identity, and future and must be prioritised as such.

title: The Council’s MFF budget proposal: bad news for AgoraEU
content:
The Cypriot Presidency has released its Negotiating Box on the next long-term EU budget (MFF), which includes proposed budget lines aimed at supporting negotiations on the MFF during upcoming European Council meetings. Unfortunately, the proposed budget allocated for AgoraEU doesn’t make for good reading.

The Council proposes an approximate 2% cut in funding when compared to the European Commission’s initial proposal. As far as the AgoraEU programme is concerned, the Council proposes a budget of €7,295 million (in constant prices), representing a 33% reduction compared to the Parliament’s position – roughly €500 million less every year for our sectors.

The budget envisaged by the Council is woefully insufficient to meet the challenges and demands facing European culture, media, democracy, and civil society.

title: Reading between the strands: AgoraEU after Parliament and Council
content:
AgoraEU, the main EU programme for culture in 2028-2034, is taking shape as the EU institutions set out their positions. Culture Action Europe explains how.

The law that will govern AgoraEU is shaped by three EU institutions: the European Commission (proposes the law), the European Parliament (amends and adopts it on behalf of EU citizens), and the Council of the EU (amends and adopts it on behalf of the 27 Member State governments).

The Commission tabled its proposal last July, merging Creative Europe and the Citizens, Equality, Rights and Values Programme (CERV) into AgoraEU. Since then, we have been waiting for the Parliament and the Council to formulate their respective positions. In May-June 2026, almost one year later, things are starting to crystallise.

title: What’s new with AgoraEU, and why does it matter?
content:
These are busy and decisive times. As the trialogue approaches, the European Parliament is working to consolidate its positions, with committees putting forward amendment after amendment on the main funding programmes that will shape the next MFF. 

Among them, AgoraEU is emerging as one of the key frameworks for supporting culture and socially impactful projects. But before diving into the details, it is worth taking a step back and asking: what’s new with AgoraEU, and why does it matter? 

On 16 July 2025, the European Commission presented its proposal for the next Multiannual Financial Framework (2028–2034), aiming for a simpler, more focused EU budget. To achieve that, one key change is the merging of existing programmes into broader, more coherent ones, and AgoraEU is one of them. 

The new programme is structured around three strands: 

  • Culture: supporting cross-border cultural creation, cooperation, and access, and reinforcing the role of the cultural and creative sectors. 
  • MEDIA+: boosting Europe’s audiovisual and video game industries, while also supporting independent journalism, media diversity, and access to reliable information.
